question: Can Transformer sequence length be scaled to 1 billion tokens by replacing quadratic attention with a linear-cost attention that stays expressive?
hypothesis: Allocating attention that decays exponentially with token distance (dilated attention) gives linear cost and log token dependency without hurting short-sequence performance.
contributions: Dilated attention: attentive field expands exponentially with distance; linear computation complexity and logarithmic dependency between tokens
Distributed training algorithm along the sequence dimension to scale to 1B tokens
Drop-in replacement for standard attention, compatible with existing Transformer optimizations
Language-modeling experiments showing strong results on long and short sequences

method.summary: Replaces self-attention in a MAGNETO/XPOS decoder with dilated attention: the sequence is split into segments of length w, each sparsified with interval r, with several (w, r) pairs mixed by softmax-denominator weights. Sequence dimension is partitioned across GPUs with an all-gather of sparsified keys/values. Evaluated on code language modeling (The Stack) against a dense Transformer and Sparse Transformer.
method.task: autoregressive language modeling (pretraining) on source code; runtime scaling benchmark

results.claim: Dilated attention has linear computation complexity O(Nd) versus O(N^2 d) for vanilla attention.
results.setup: Analytical derivation (Eq 16-18), geometric w and r

results.claim: Token dependency (maximum path length) is approximately logarithmic in sequence length.
results.quote: This proves that the token dependency is approximate to O(log N).

results.claim: Dilated attention keeps almost constant latency as sequence length grows to 1B tokens while vanilla attention latency rises quadratically.
results.setup: Forward pass, both with FlashAttention, 8K to 1B tokens, distributed over GPUs, up to 3 segment lengths (2,048, tokens per device, sequence length); average of 10 runs
results.quote: It shows that dilated attention can successfully scale up the sequence length with almost constant latency.
results.note: Per-length values only in Fig 5; GPU count not stated

results.claim: At test length 32K, LONGNET trained at 32K reaches perplexity 3.01 versus 3.64 for Sparse Transformer trained at 32K.
results.setup: 125M-scale base config, The Stack, trained 300K steps at 0.5M tokens per batch, train length 32K, test length 32K
results.table: Table 2, row LONGNET (ours) Length 32K, column Github 32K
results.note: Sparse Transformer 3.64 from Table 2 row Sparse Transformer 32K

results.claim: Dense Transformer trained at 2K degrades badly when tested at 32K by extrapolation (11.29 PPL), against LONGNET trained at 32K (3.01).
results.setup: Test length 32K with blockwise causal attention for the 2K-trained dense Transformer

results.claim: At the shortest test length (2K), LONGNET trained at 8K matches the dense Transformer (4.23 vs 4.24 PPL).
results.setup: Test length 2K, LONGNET trained at 8K vs Transformer trained at 2K
results.note: Longer training length raises 2K perplexity: LONGNET 4.27 (16K), 4.37 (32K)

results.claim: LONGNET reaches lower test loss than dense Transformers with less compute across training lengths.
results.setup: Training lengths 2K to 32K, test lengths 1K-32K with BCA
results.quote: LONGNET outperforms dense Transformers with a lower perplexity and a significantly smaller amount of computation.

results.claim: LONGNET follows a power-law scaling curve from 125M to 2.7B parameters.
results.quote: This implies that the dense Transformer is not a prerequisite for scaling the language models.

results.claim: Longer prompt context lowers suffix test loss.
results.setup: Prompt prefix length 2K to 32K, same suffix
results.quote: It shows that the test loss of LONGNET gradually decreases as the context window grows.

results.claim: Dilated attention cuts computation versus vanilla attention by a factor of N/w r^2.
results.quote: Dilated attention can significantly reduce the computation cost by a factor of N
results.note: Text extraction splits the formula N/(w) r^2

limits: Only evaluated on code (The Stack) language modeling; no natural-language, downstream or retrieval benchmarks.
1B-token claim rests on a runtime benchmark (Fig 5), not a trained model; models were trained at up to 32K only.
Extrapolation at inference does not work when length is much larger than the model supports (authors).
Baseline dense Transformer only scaled to 32K for compute reasons; the Table 2 cells vary train and test length together.
No seeds, variance, hardware, GPU count or wall-clock stated; dataset size not stated.
Future work lists multimodal, BEiT pretraining and genomic data, so these are untested.

terms.definition: Splits (Q,K,V) into segments of length w and sparsifies each by selecting rows with interval r; attention is computed on the sparsified segments then scattered back.
